title: Peeling Tape in a Vacuum Makes X-Rays, Enough to Image a Finger

scenes.text: Peeling sticky tape can make X-rays.
scenes.keywords: sticky tape roll peeling close up

scenes.text: Not in your kitchen. Inside a vacuum chamber, where there's no air.
Researchers at UCLA peeled the tape and detected bursts of X-rays, each lasting about a billionth of a second.
They used the glow to take an X-ray picture of a researcher's finger.
It was published in the journal Nature in 2008. Let air back in, and the X-rays vanish.
An X-ray machine, from a roll of tape.

description:
Peeling ordinary sticky tape inside a vacuum can give off X-rays.
Researchers at UCLA detected pulses lasting about a billionth of a second and used them to image a finger. With air present, no X-rays are produced.
What other everyday thing do you think hides a surprise like this? Comment below.
first_comment: The effect only happens in a vacuum. If you could test one everyday object in a vacuum chamber, what would you pick?
